title: SSO
summary: Single sign-on (SSO) is an authentication architecture in which one identity provider authenticates a principal once and then issues assertions or tokens that multiple relying-party applications accept in place of their own credential stores. Instead of every application holding a password database, each application trusts a federated identity provider such as Entra ID, Okta, Ping or a Keycloak deployment, and receives a signed statement about who the user is and, increasingly, what context the authentication occurred in. The security benefit is concentrated and easy to understate: credentials live in one hardened location with one MFA policy, one lockout policy, one session lifetime and one revocation path, so deprovisioning a leaver becomes a single disable action rather than a hunt through dozens of local account stores. The corresponding risk is that the identity provider becomes a tier-zero system whose compromise grants access to every federated application, and that the session cookie or refresh token becomes the real credential that adversaries pursue. Most real-world SSO incidents therefore involve token theft, consent phishing against the authorisation endpoint, misconfigured assertion validation on the relying-party side, or stale accounts that survive offboarding because a shadow application was never federated. Practitioners must be able to reason about session lifetime, token binding, sign-out propagation, identifier normalisation and the difference between an application that validates a signature correctly and one that merely decodes it. Logging quality matters here: the identity provider's sign-in and audit logs, not the application logs, are usually the authoritative record of who authenticated and from where.
objectives: You will be able to explain the roles of identity provider, service provider and relying party in a federated sign-in flow.
You will be able to describe why the SSO session token, not the password, is the primary credential an adversary targets.
You will be able to evaluate session lifetime, token binding and global sign-out settings against a stated risk appetite.
You will be able to identify common SSO misconfigurations such as unvalidated assertions, wildcard redirect URIs and orphaned application accounts.
You will be able to use identity provider sign-in logs to reconstruct an authentication timeline for incident response.
You will be able to plan deprovisioning so that disabling one identity revokes access to all federated applications.
